subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage: In the courtyard of a mud-walled house, two-year-old Neelam was banging a steel spoon on an upturned bowl. Her mother Swati, hands floury from the morning rotis, gently lifted the spoon away. Neelam's eyebrows dropped, her lower lip pushed out, and she glared at the spoon in Swati's fingers. Swati crouched down. “You're cross. You wanted the spoon.” Neelam sniffed, leaned her whole weight against Swati's knee, still pouting, and lifted both arms to be picked up.

qa.q: What did Swati take away from Neelam?
qa.a: A steel spoon that Neelam had been banging on an upturned bowl.

qa.q: What might Neelam have been feeling when she lifted her arms, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: Most likely she felt frustrated about losing the spoon and wanted comfort, since she leaned on Swati and asked to be held. Another reading is that she was simply tired and wanted to be carried. 🙂

qa.q: What small step could Swati take next?
qa.a: She could keep naming the feeling in simple words, hold Neelam for a moment, and then offer a different safe thing to bang, such as a wooden spoon.

qa.q: How might Swati see Neelam's pout?
qa.a: Swati is likely to see it as a young child's honest signal of being upset and wanting closeness, not as a plan to get her way.

grounding: The toddler's frown and pout after the spoon is taken shows frustration and a wish for comfort, and the mother names the feeling.

subtype: Frown, scowl and pout in frustration [Expressing]
passage: Tomas, twenty months old, was filling a red bucket with sand at the park when an older boy scooped it up to carry to the water tap. Tomas's brows drew together, his mouth turned down, and his lip stuck out as he stared after the bucket. Then he turned and looked at his father. Mateo knelt beside him. “That was your bucket, and you're frustrated.” Tomas kept scowling but toddled into Mateo's arms and stayed there until the boy brought the bucket back.

qa.q: Where was Tomas when his bucket was taken?
qa.a: At the park, where he was filling a red bucket with sand.

qa.q: What does Tomas's look toward his father suggest he wanted?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted comfort or help, and the scowl shows frustration. It could also have been plain surprise at the sudden loss, since he had no time to react before the boy walked off.

qa.q: What could Mateo try if the bucket had not come back?
qa.a: He could keep naming the feeling, stay close, and steer Tomas gently toward another digging toy so the upset has somewhere to go.

qa.q: What might the older boy have been thinking?
qa.a: He may have thought the bucket was free to use and not realised Tomas minded. Bringing it back suggests he noticed Tomas's face and father.

grounding: The toddler scowls and pouts when his bucket is taken, and the father names the frustration and offers comfort.

subtype: Grimace and wince at pain or taste [Expressing]
passage: From my balcony I saw little Sunaina, about two, take a mouthful of bitter gourd from her plate. Her nose wrinkled, her eyes squeezed shut and her tongue pushed the food out. A minute later she ran towards the door, tripped on the step and winced, clutching her knee. Nandini here, her neighbour; I can't say what was in her head. But the first face looked like taste, and the second looked like a real bump. Her mother checked the knee, found a red mark, and gave her water.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do after eating the bitter gourd?
qa.a: Her nose wrinkled, her eyes squeezed shut and she pushed the food out with her tongue.

qa.q: How does Nandini read Sunaina's two faces, and what else might they mean?
qa.a: She reads the first as a reaction to the bitter taste and the second as pain from the bump, because each followed something that happened. She admits she cannot know Sunaina's thoughts, and either face could also mean plain surprise.

qa.q: What did Sunaina's mother do well, and what else could she do?
qa.a: She looked at the knee instead of assuming a tantrum. She could also hug Sunaina and, if the leg still bothered her, check with a doctor. 🤍

qa.q: What might the moment look like from Sunaina's mother's side?
qa.a: She would see two similar grimaces with different causes, so she needs to look at the situation each time before deciding whether her daughter is hurt or just tasting something strong.

grounding: The toddler's grimace after a bitter taste and a wince after a bump are read with the situation, and the knee is checked.

subtype: Grimace and wince at pain or taste [Expressing]
passage: Monday: Harsha's son Uday, nearly two, bit into a slice of raw lemon and screwed up his whole face, then stared at the lemon. Wednesday: he bumped his shin on the low table, winced and went silent. Harsha lifted his trouser leg, found only a pink patch, and rubbed it gently. Saturday: Harsha offered lemon again. Uday scrunched his eyes, shook his head, and then reached for a second slice anyway, grimacing all over again. Harsha laughed. “Sour, yes? Face says so.”

qa.q: On which day did Uday bump his shin?
qa.a: On Wednesday, on the low table.

qa.q: What was Uday probably feeling on Saturday when he took a second slice?
qa.a: Probably he found the sour taste startling but was curious enough to try again, as the grimace and the reaching hand show together. Another possibility is that he wanted to copy Harsha's laugh.

qa.q: What did Harsha do that helped on Wednesday?
qa.a: He looked at the shin and found only a pink patch instead of assuming Uday was fussing. If the leg had looked swollen or Uday kept crying, he could have asked a doctor.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Uday reaching for a second slice on Saturday?
qa.a: Harsha seems amused and fond, laughing and naming the sour face, and may be pleased that Uday is brave enough to try again.

grounding: A toddler's reflexive grimace at a sour taste and wince after a bump are read with the situation and the injury is checked.

subtype: Open-mouthed surprise or wonder [Expressing]
passage: Jeevan, seventeen months, was at the third-floor window of the flat when a cow ambled down the colony lane. His mouth fell open. He stood very still, one hand gripping the grille, eyes fixed on the huge brown shape. Rashmi, his mother, came up behind him and smiled. “Cow. Look, a gentle cow.” Just then a scooter horn blared below and Jeevan jerked, then peered up at his mother's calm face. His mouth slowly closed into a small, wobbly grin, and he pointed.

qa.q: What did Jeevan see from the window?
qa.a: A cow walking down the colony lane.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have felt when his mouth fell open, and what else could it be?
qa.a: It could be wonder at seeing something so big, as his fixed stare and pointing show. It could also have been the start of fear, since he gripped the grille and froze when the horn sounded.

qa.q: What made it easier for Jeevan to settle?
qa.a: Rashmi's calm smile and simple words gave him something to read. She could also stay beside him and keep naming what he sees.

qa.q: What might Rashmi be noticing about her son?
qa.a: She might see that he looks to her face when something surprising happens, and that her own calm helps him choose how to feel. 🙂

grounding: A toddler's open-mouthed stare at a new animal and a sudden noise could be wonder, startle or fear, and a caregiver's calm face helps.

subtype: Open-mouthed surprise or wonder [Expressing]
passage:
“Kiran! Look at your face,” said Baljeet. “Mouth wide open. What do you see?”
“Big,” Kiran whispered, pointing at the garden.
“That's Nani's tortoise. He's slow.”
Kiran stepped back and grabbed her father's trouser leg. “Bite?”
“No biting. Watch, he's eating a leaf.” Baljeet crouched and smiled.
“Nani, is he friendly?” he called.
“Very,” said Nani from the veranda.
Kiran peeked round his knee, mouth still open. “Leaf,” she said, and let go of the trouser.

qa.q: Whose tortoise was in the garden?
qa.a: It was Nani's tortoise, and Nani called from the veranda.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when she asked “Bite?”
qa.a: She seemed a little afraid, shown by stepping back and gripping her father's trouser leg. Her open mouth and stare could also mean she was fascinated, so probably she felt both.

qa.q: How did Baljeet help Kiran decide what to feel?
qa.a: He stayed calm, smiled, explained the tortoise was eating a leaf, and checked with Nani. He might also let her watch from a distance until she is ready.

qa.q: If Baljeet had jumped back and looked alarmed, what might have changed for Kiran?
qa.a: She might have taken his alarm as proof the animal was dangerous and become more frightened, rather than curious.

grounding: A toddler's open-mouthed look at a new animal mixes wonder and possible fear, and the caregiver's calm face settles it.

subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage: The daycare door in Helsinki opened at four and Kaito, nineteen months old, was sitting on the mat with a wooden puzzle. He looked up. Sami stood in the doorway, still in his cycling jacket. Kaito's whole face opened into a wide smile, cheeks round, eyes crinkled, and he dropped the puzzle piece and ran with his arms out. “Hello, you,” said Sami, scooping him up. Kaito patted his father's cheek and kept smiling, then pointed back at the puzzle to show him.

qa.q: Where did Sami pick up Kaito?
qa.a: At the daycare in Helsinki, at four o'clock.

qa.q: What does Kaito's smile tell you about how he feels toward Sami?
qa.a: It suggests delight and closeness, since he smiled, dropped the piece and ran straight to him. It is a natural greeting for his age rather than a hidden plan.

qa.q: What could Sami do next to keep the connection going?
qa.a: He could look at the puzzle with Kaito, smile back and say what he sees, giving the happy moment some words. 😊

qa.q: How might the daycare staff see Kaito's greeting?
qa.a: They may see a child who is securely attached and glad to be reunited, which tells them he feels safe with his father.

grounding: A toddler beams at a familiar caregiver, showing delight and attachment without any hidden purpose.

subtype: Smile and beam as social signal [Expressing]
passage: Our lane's little Pallavi, about two, sits on her doorstep every evening waiting. I watch from my window. When her father Uday rounds the corner on his bicycle, she beams, kicks both feet and calls “Papa!” She does it the same way for her grandfather and, I noticed, for the milk-delivery man once, who happened to wave. I can't tell exactly what she thinks. To me it looks like plain gladness at a friendly, familiar face, nothing sly about it.

qa.q: Where does Pallavi sit each evening?
qa.a: On her doorstep, waiting for her father to come around the corner.

qa.q: What does the narrator think Pallavi's beam means, and what is left uncertain?
qa.a: The narrator thinks it is plain gladness at a friendly, familiar face, seen in the kicking feet and the call of “Papa”. She admits she cannot know exactly what Pallavi is thinking.

qa.q: What could Uday do when he sees the smile?
qa.a: He could get off the bicycle, smile back and greet her by name so the happy moment is shared. 😊

qa.q: What might the milk-delivery man feel when Pallavi beams at him?
qa.a: He may feel pleasantly surprised and welcomed, since a toddler's smile is easy to take as a small greeting even from a passer-by.

grounding: A toddler beams at familiar people as an open social signal of delight, seen by a neighbour who cannot be sure of her thoughts.

subtype: Social smile emerging [Expressing]
passage: Creche note, Thursday. Farhan has just turned one and joined our room this month. This week I noticed him light up with a wide smile, mouth open, when I bent over his mat, and again when the cook, Mala, called his name from the door. Each time I smiled back and said, “Hello, Farhan,” and he answered with a gurgle, then looked at me again as if waiting. I will keep greeting him face to face at his level. 🙂 Ganga

qa.q: Who wrote the note, and when?
qa.a: Ganga, signing at the end, wrote the creche note on Thursday.

qa.q: What might Farhan's wide smile and waiting look mean?
qa.a: Probably pleasure and a wish to keep the exchange going, since he smiled, gurgled and looked back at her. He might also just be reacting to a friendly tone of voice.

qa.q: What is Ganga's plan and why might it work?
qa.a: She will greet him face to face at his level. Smiling back gives him a response, which helps him learn that his signals get answered.

qa.q: How might Mala's greeting feel to Farhan?
qa.a: Hearing his name from a familiar voice can feel welcoming, so he smiles at her too, showing he already links her with warmth.

grounding: A young child gives broad social smiles to familiar faces, and the adult's returned smile builds the exchange.

subtype: Social smile emerging [Expressing]
passage: On the verandah in the afternoon light, Swati sat with her baby Yogesh in her lap, wiping his face after his rice. He looked up at her and his mouth opened into a huge, gummy smile, arms waving. Swati smiled back and tilted her head. “Oh, is that for me?” Yogesh cooed and smiled again, watching her eyes. Her mother-in-law, passing with a basket, grinned at the pair. Swati waited a beat, then said his name softly and got another smile in return, like a small back-and-forth.

qa.q: What was Swati doing when Yogesh smiled at her?
qa.a: She was wiping his face after his rice while he sat in her lap on the verandah.

qa.q: What does Yogesh seem to feel when he smiles at Swati?
qa.a: He seems pleased and connected to her, since he waves his arms and keeps watching her eyes. It could also be a response to her friendly voice, not yet a message meant for her.

qa.q: Why does Swati's smiling back matter?
qa.a: It shows him that his signal gets an answer, and it starts a conversation of attention. She can keep taking small turns with him.

qa.q: How might Swati's mother-in-law see the moment?
qa.a: She may see a mother and baby learning each other, and it may bring back memories of her own children's first smiles.

grounding: A young child gives a broad open-mouth smile to a familiar face, and the mother's smile back builds the early back-and-forth.

subtype: Sustained and fleeting smiles in play [Expressing]
passage: At my cousin's naming-day gathering I watched Rashmi, about two, with her uncle Yash on the sofa. He hid behind a cushion and popped out; her mouth flickered into a tiny smile that vanished in a second, and she looked straight back at the cushion. Later he chased her round the low table and her smile stayed wide for a long stretch, with squeals. I don't know exactly what goes on in her head, but the short smile didn't seem like boredom. She kept asking him with her eyes to go again.

qa.q: What game did Yash play that got a wide, lasting smile from Rashmi?
qa.a: He chased her round the low table.

qa.q: What does the narrator think Rashmi's brief smile at the cushion means?
qa.a: She reads it as quick joy or surprise, not boredom, because Rashmi kept looking back at the cushion and wanted more. The narrator admits she cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Yash do next?
qa.a: He could repeat the cushion trick a few times and follow Rashmi's lead, going longer if she stays interested and stopping when she looks away.

qa.q: What might Rashmi's parents think if they saw only the short smile?
qa.a: They might worry she was not enjoying it, but seeing the eager look and the longer smile in the chase would show that brief smiles are simply how her joy sometimes appears.

grounding: A toddler shows a fleeting smile at a peekaboo surprise and a sustained smile in a favourite game, and the observer does not read the short smile as disinterest.

subtype: Sustained and fleeting smiles in play [Expressing]
passage: Monday: Harish held a napkin over his face and pulled it away. Ojas, twenty months, flashed a quick smile, gone in a blink, and pointed at the napkin. Harish worried he wasn't enjoying it. Wednesday, at the park: Harish began the tickle-chase, and Ojas smiled wide and kept smiling, squealing, all the way to the slide. Friday: the napkin came out again. Same flicker of a smile, then a grab for the napkin to cover Harish's face instead. Harish laughed, relieved. “So that's how you laugh at this one.”

qa.q: Where did Harish play the tickle-chase with Ojas?
qa.a: At the park, ending at the slide.

qa.q: Why was Harish relieved on Friday?
qa.a: He saw that Ojas's short smile came with wanting to play more, since Ojas grabbed the napkin. That showed the flicker was real enjoyment, though it could also have been simple curiosity about the napkin.

qa.q: What could Harish do with what he learned?
qa.a: He could keep offering short surprise games and long chasing games, letting Ojas set the pace instead of judging a game by how long the smile lasts.

qa.q: How might Ojas see the change on Friday?
qa.a: Grabbing the napkin lets him be the one who makes the surprise, so he may feel like an equal player in the game rather than an audience. 😊

grounding: A toddler shows a fleeting smile at peekaboo and a sustained one in a favourite game, both normal signs of joy.

subtype: Brow raise in surprise and attention [Expressing]
passage:
“Parul, listen,” said Vasudha, “what's this?” She squeezed a rubber duck and it gave a loud squeak.
Parul's eyebrows shot up and her eyes went round. “Uh!”
“Was that a funny sound?”
“More,” said Parul.
Squeak.
Her eyebrows went up again and she giggled. Vasudha's husband called from the kitchen, “What's she laughing at?”
“The duck! Her whole forehead moves.”
“Do it again.”
Squeak. Parul's brows lifted, then she reached for the duck herself.

qa.q: What object made the sound Parul liked?
qa.a: A rubber duck that Vasudha squeezed so that it squeaked.

qa.q: What does Parul's raised forehead show, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It most likely shows surprise and interest, since she asked for “More” and giggled. It could also be a brief startle, but her reaching for the duck points toward enjoyment.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do next?
qa.a: She could hand Parul the duck and let her squeeze it herself, naming her surprise and delight in a few words.

qa.q: How might Vasudha's husband see the moment from the kitchen?
qa.a: He hears the laughter without the face, so Vasudha's description helps him picture the raised brows, and he may join in when he sees it himself.

grounding: A toddler raises both eyebrows at a funny sound, showing surprise and interest, seen in a home scene.

subtype: Brow raise in surprise and attention [Expressing]
passage: Playgroup observation, Tuesday. Lakshmi, about two and a half, sat with a toy xylophone. When Ms. Rao's shoes squeaked across the floor she lifted both eyebrows high and turned her head. She looked at the shoes, then at me, and copied the squeak with her mouth. I did not tell her what to feel. I squeaked my own shoe on the floor and smiled, and she laughed. Her brows went up again each time. Later I told her mother about the squeaky shoes so she could try it at home. 🙂

qa.q: What sound made Lakshmi raise her eyebrows?
qa.a: The squeak of Ms. Rao's shoes on the floor.

qa.q: What is Lakshmi likely feeling when her brows lift, and what else is possible?
qa.a: She is likely surprised and interested, since she looks at the shoes, imitates the sound and laughs. It could also have been a moment of mild alarm, but her laughter suggests otherwise.

qa.q: What did the observer do that supported Lakshmi?
qa.a: They let Lakshmi enjoy the surprise, joined in with their own squeak and shared the idea with Lakshmi's mother so the play could continue at home.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's mother feel hearing about the shoes?
qa.a: She may feel glad to know what makes her daughter light up and pleased to have a simple game to try, and she might enjoy watching those raised brows herself.

grounding: A toddler raises her eyebrows at a funny sound as an early reflexive sign of surprise and interest, noted by a teacher.

subtype: Furrowed brow in effort or upset [Expressing]
passage: Day one: Tanvir, two, was stacking building blocks when the tower toppled. His brow creased tight and Sudha thought he was angry. He whispered, “Again.” Day two: the same tower leaned, his forehead folded and his lip trembled, and Sudha crouched. “Shall I hold the bottom?” She held it steady and he finished. Day three: Tanvir built four blocks high, tongue out, brow furrowed in complete focus, and did not look up when Sudha called him for tea.

qa.q: How many blocks did Tanvir stack on the third day?
qa.a: Four blocks.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's furrowed brow mean on each day?
qa.a: On day one it seems to be frustration mixed with effort since he said “Again”. On day two it showed distress before crying, and on day three it showed pure concentration. Sudha's first guess of anger was one possible reading.

qa.q: What worked in how Sudha responded on day two?
qa.a: She checked the situation and offered a small piece of help without taking over, so Tanvir finished the tower himself.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Sudha's help?
qa.a: He may feel supported and understood, and confident enough to keep trying because his mother stayed close but let him do the building. 😊

grounding: A toddler furrows the brow while concentrating or before crying, and the mother checks the situation and helps rather than assuming anger.

subtype: Furrowed brow in effort or upset [Expressing]
passage: Lalit sat on the floor of the flat with his granddaughter Chaitanya, who was two and a half, and her shoe. She pushed her foot at it again and again. Her forehead wrinkled deep and her lips pressed together. Lalit began to say “Are you angry?” but stopped. She pushed harder, then made a small whimper. “That shoe is stubborn,” said Lalit, and held the heel open. Her brow smoothed as the foot slid in. “Mine,” she said. Lalit handed her the other shoe and let her try alone.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya trying to do?
qa.a: She kept pushing her foot at her shoe.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya's wrinkled forehead most likely show, and what else might it show?
qa.a: Most likely effort and rising frustration, since she pressed her lips and whimpered when it did not work. It could also be a sign of being tired or about to cry.

qa.q: What could Lalit do the next time she struggles?
qa.a: He could wait a moment, then offer small help such as holding the heel, and let her do the last part.

qa.q: What might Lalit's first thought of anger have caused if he had said it aloud?
qa.a: Chaitanya might have felt misunderstood, since her upset was about the shoe and not about him.

grounding: A toddler furrows her brow in effort and near-upset over a shoe, and the adult offers help instead of assuming anger.

subtype: Squeezing eyes shut and blinking [Expressing]
passage: At the temple fair, Tejas, two, sat on his grandfather Hrithik's shoulders as a drummer in a bright mask stepped near. Tejas squeezed his eyes tight shut and buried his face in Hrithik's grey hair. “Not looking,” he mumbled. Hrithik walked to a quiet corner and said nothing more. Later, among the sweet stalls, Tejas's blinks grew slow and heavy. His head sank onto Hrithik's shoulder and his eyes closed. Hrithik headed home, patting the small back.

qa.q: Where was Tejas when the masked drummer came close?
qa.a: On his grandfather Hrithik's shoulders at the temple fair.

qa.q: Why did Tejas squeeze his eyes shut, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: Most likely he was scared by the mask and drum, since he hid his face and said “Not looking”. It could also be that the noise and crowd were too much, which is a different kind of overwhelm.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that helped?
qa.a: He moved to a quiet corner and did not push Tejas to look, which lets a frightened child settle in his own time.

qa.q: How might the drummer see a child hiding his face?
qa.a: He may realise the costume looks big and frightening to a small child, and could give a friendly wave from a distance rather than take offence.

grounding: A toddler squeezes his eyes shut when scared and later blinks slowly when sleepy, protective and tired signals rather than defiance.

subtype: Squeezing eyes shut and blinking [Expressing]
passage: Pablo lifted his daughter Zeynep out of the bath and reached for the shampoo. She clamped her eyes shut, scrunched her nose and turned her face into the towel. “Eyes closed, I can see,” said Pablo, and poured water only on her back. In the car later, the streetlights slid past and her eyelids began to droop. Each blink lasted longer than the one before. Pablo lowered the radio. By the time they parked in front of the flats, Zeynep was asleep, her fingers loosely holding the blanket.

qa.q: What did Pablo reach for that made Zeynep close her eyes?
qa.a: The shampoo.

qa.q: What do Zeynep's closed eyes at bath time suggest, and what might be another reading?
qa.a: They suggest she is worried about the shampoo, since she also turned her face away. Another reading is that she was tired and simply did not want to look.

qa.q: What did Pablo do that respected Zeynep's signal?
qa.a: He poured water on her back and left her face alone, and later kept the car quiet when her blinks slowed with sleep.

qa.q: What might bath time be like for Zeynep?
qa.a: It may feel like a slippery, loud moment where she cannot control what comes next, so shutting her eyes gives her a small way to feel safe.

grounding: A toddler squeezes her eyes shut at a feared moment and blinks slowly when sleepy, both protective or tired signals.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage: Park note, Monday. Mehak, nearly two, was sitting in the sandpit when a large brown dog trotted by on a lead. Her eyes went wide and she went still. Then she turned and looked straight at my face. I kept my voice calm, smiled and said, “That's a dog, and his owner is holding him.” Her shoulders dropped, and she pointed. I stayed beside her while she watched him leave. Next time we will watch from further away first and see how she feels. 🙂

qa.q: Where was Mehak when the dog passed?
qa.a: In the sandpit at the park.

qa.q: Why did Mehak look at the narrator's face after seeing the dog?
qa.a: She was probably checking whether the dog was safe, and her wide eyes could show fascination or alarm. Her dropped shoulders after the narrator's calm words suggest she felt reassured.

qa.q: What is the narrator's plan for next time and why is it sensible?
qa.a: They will start further from the dog and see how Mehak reacts. That lets Mehak approach the new sight at her own pace.

qa.q: How might the dog owner's calm hold on the lead matter to Mehak?
qa.a: Seeing the lead may help Mehak feel the dog is under control, and the owner's relaxed manner adds to the narrator's calm message.

grounding: A toddler widens her eyes at something new and checks the caregiver's face to decide between wonder and alarm.

subtype: Wide eyes in wonder and fear [Expressing]
passage: A peacock stepped onto the mud path in front of the house, fanning half its tail. Charu, two, stopped with her eyes stretched wide. She held her breath and looked at the huge bird, then swung round to see her aunt Lavanya's face. Lavanya was smiling at the peacock. “Mor,” she said softly. Charu's shoulders dropped, and she took one careful step towards it, then another, eyes still wide, one hand reaching behind her for the edge of Lavanya's saree.

qa.q: What did Charu see on the mud path?
qa.a: A peacock with its tail half fanned.

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when she looked back at Lavanya, and what could it mean otherwise?
qa.a: She was probably checking whether the peacock was safe. Her wide eyes could mean fascination or a little alarm, and her stepping forward while holding the saree suggests both.

qa.q: What could Lavanya do to help Charu enjoy the moment?
qa.a: She could stay close, keep her calm smile, and let Charu decide how near to go.

qa.q: What might have happened if Lavanya had looked frightened?
qa.a: Charu might have taken it as a sign the bird was dangerous and backed away, so the wonder could have turned into fear.

grounding: A toddler widens her eyes at something new and looks to the caregiver for a reaction to decide between wonder and fear.
